solution.concept_anchor: 42nd Amendment transfer of Education to Concurrent List
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who know Education was once a State subject assume it remains there, failing to register the 42nd Amendment's centralising shift.
elimination_logic: Eliminate options placing Education in the State List — the 42nd Amendment (1976) transferred it to the Concurrent List (Entry 25).
Eliminate any option claiming residuary power rests with states — Article 248 vests residuary power exclusively in Parliament.
Confirm: Education (Entry 25), Forests (Entry 17A), and Weights & Measures were all moved to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment — option (b) is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who have partial knowledge know that Education was originally a State List subject. The 42nd Amendment (1976), enacted during the Emergency, transferred Education to the Concurrent List. Many students continue to associate Education with the State List, which is the single most common misconception tested in this sub-topic. Option (a) is deliberately placed first to capture this large category of partially prepared candidates.
solution.final_explanation:
The Seventh Schedule divides legislative subjects across three lists. The 42nd Constitutional Amendment (1976) made significant centralist changes by moving several subjects from the State List to the Concurrent List.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Education is NOT in the State List. It was transferred to the Concurrent List as Entry 25 by the 42nd Amendment.
• Option (b) — Correct: Education (Entry 25), Forests (Entry 17A), Protection of Wild Animals and Birds (Entry 17B), and Weights & Measures are currently in the Concurrent List — all transferred from the State List by the 42nd Amendment.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Forests are in the Concurrent List, not the Union List.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Residuary power rests with Parliament under Article 248 read with Entry 97, not with states.

Value Addition:
• The NEP 2020 derives part of its constitutional basis from Education being a Concurrent List subject.
• Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions both recommended partial restoration of these subjects to the State List.
• Currently: Union List — 100 entries; State List — 61 entries; Concurrent List — 52 entries.

Repugnancy Doctrine: Article 254 and Centre-State Concurrent List Conflict

solution.concept_anchor: Article 254 repugnancy — Concurrent List conflict rules

statement_analysis.statement: The doctrine of repugnancy under Article 254 applies equally to conflicts between Central and State laws on both the Union List and the Concurrent List.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 254 applies ONLY to the Concurrent List. When Parliament legislates on the Union List, the issue is one of legislative competence, not repugnancy. States have no power to legislate on Union List subjects in the first place.

statement_analysis.statement: Once a State law on the Concurrent List receives Presidential assent under Article 254(2), Parliament loses its power to subsequently pass a law overriding that State law.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 254(2) allows the State law to prevail, but Parliament retains full power to later enact a law on the same subject that will override the State law. The Presidential assent gives temporary supremacy, not permanent immunity.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the 'occupied field' doctrine, a State law may be rendered void by a Central law on the Concurrent List even if there is no direct contradiction between the two laws.
statement_analysis.reason: The occupied field test can void a State law even without direct conflict, if Parliament has comprehensively covered the field intending no further legislation — as established in Zaverbhai Amaidas v. State of Bombay.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who correctly identify Statement 1 as incorrect may assume Statement 2 is correct (believing Presidential assent creates a permanent shield), leading them to select (d) which excludes Statement 3.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: Article 254 is explicitly confined to the Concurrent List — it does not apply to Union List conflicts. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Check Statement 2: Article 254(2) Presidential assent does not strip Parliament of future override power — Parliament can legislate subsequently to prevail. Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Check Statement 3: Occupied field doctrine can void a state law without direct contradiction — this is settled law (Zaverbhai case). Statement 3 IS correct.
Statements 1 and 2 are NOT correct — the answer asking for incorrect statements is (b): 1 and 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the primary trap. Many students believe Presidential assent under Article 254(2) creates an absolute shield for State laws. In reality, Parliament retains the power to subsequently legislate and override even a Presidential assent-protected State law. This is a scope-extension trap — the protection is real but students incorrectly extend it to mean 'permanent immunity from Parliament.'
solution.final_explanation:
Article 254 governs repugnancy between Central and State laws on the Concurrent List. Two key misconceptions are tested here.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 254 operates exclusively on the Concurrent List. Union List conflicts are a matter of legislative incompetence of states, not repugnancy. A state simply has no power to legislate on Union List subjects.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Presidential assent under Article 254(2) allows a State law to prevail over a prior Central law, but Parliament can subsequently enact a new law that overrides the assented State law. The assent creates no permanent bar on Parliament.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The occupied field doctrine extends beyond direct contradiction. If Parliament comprehensively legislates intending to cover an entire field, a State law is void even if not directly contradictory — established in Zaverbhai Amaidas v. State of Bombay.

Value Addition:
• The two tests for repugnancy are: (i) direct conflict test and (ii) occupied field test — both from M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India.
• A State law saved by Article 254(2) remains state law — it does not become Central law.
• Repugnancy voids State law only 'to the extent of repugnancy' — the rest of the State law survives.

Parliamentary Legislation on State List: Article 253 (International Treaties)

solution.concept_anchor: Articles 252 and 253 — distinguishing features

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 252, Parliament can legislate on a State List subject if two or more state legislatures pass resolutions requesting Parliament to do so.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the precise mechanism of Article 252 — state legislature resolutions requesting Parliamentary legislation on a State List subject.

statement_analysis.statement: A law enacted by Parliament under Article 252 can be amended by any of the consenting states unilaterally after Parliament has enacted it.
statement_analysis.reason: Once Parliament legislates under Article 252, the consenting states CANNOT repeal or amend that law. Only Parliament can amend it. This irrevocability is a key feature of Article 252.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 253 requires prior consent of affected state governments before Parliament can legislate to implement an international treaty on a State List subject.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 253 requires NO state consent whatsoever. Parliament can unilaterally legislate on any subject, including State List subjects, to implement international treaties, agreements, or conventions.

statement_analysis.statement: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 was enacted by Parliament pursuant to resolutions passed by state legislatures invoking Article 252.
statement_analysis.reason: The Water Act 1974 is a real-world example of Article 252 legislation — state legislatures passed resolutions requesting Parliament to legislate on what is ordinarily a state subject.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 4 as correct may hesitate on Statement 3, believing Article 253 requires at least some consultation with states, leading them to mark three statements correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — Article 252 is explicitly triggered by state legislature resolutions.
Statement 2 is incorrect — consenting states lose the power to amend or repeal once Parliament acts; only Parliament can modify the law.
Statement 3 is incorrect — Article 253 requires no state consent at all; it is a unilateral Union power to implement international obligations.
Statement 4 is correct — Water Act 1974 is a standard Article 252 example. Only two statements (1 and 4) are correct — answer is (a) Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the primary trap. Students often conflate Article 252 (state-initiated, requires state consent) with Article 253 (Union-initiated, no state consent needed). The question pairs these two articles to force precise distinction. A student who believes Article 253 also requires some form of state consent will mark three statements as correct and choose (b) instead of (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 252 and 253 both allow Parliament to legislate on State List subjects but through fundamentally different triggers and with different implications for state autonomy.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 252 is activated when two or more state legislatures pass resolutions requesting Parliamentary legislation on a State List subject.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The irrevocability feature of Article 252 means consenting states surrender amendment/repeal power once Parliament acts. Only Parliament can subsequently modify the law.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Article 253 is the most centralising provision — Parliament can legislate on ANY subject (including State List) to implement international treaties without any state consent.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 is the textbook example of Article 252 legislation, along with the Prize Competition Act, 1955.

Value Addition:
• Non-consenting states can later adopt Article 252 legislation by passing a similar resolution in their legislatures.
• Article 253 covers treaties, agreements, AND conventions — a broader scope than commonly assumed.
• Climate commitments (Paris Agreement) and WTO/TRIPS obligations can override state powers under Article 253.

solution.concept_anchor: Sunset clauses — Articles 250, 252, 357 compared
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know that Article 250 laws lapse 6 months after emergency may apply the same logic to Article 357 laws, conflating their sunset rules.
elimination_logic: Match A (Article 250): Laws cease to operate 6 months after National Emergency ceases — this matches description 3.
Match B (Article 252): Only consenting states are bound; non-consenting states can adopt by resolution — this matches description 1.
Match C (Article 249): Resolution is valid for 1 year, renewable; law lapses 6 months after resolution expires — this matches description 4.

Match D (Article 357): Laws made during President's Rule continue after President's Rule ends unless repealed by the state — this matches description 2. Correct combination: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap lies in confusing the sunset clauses of Articles 250 and 357. Both deal with emergency-related legislative expansion, but their post-emergency fate is opposite: Article 250 laws lapse 6 months after the National Emergency ends, while Article 357 laws survive indefinitely after President's Rule unless the state legislature repeals them. Students who apply one rule to both will swap entries A and D.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests precise knowledge of four distinct provisions that expand Parliamentary competence over State List subjects, with different triggers and post-expiry consequences.

• A-3 (Article 250): During National Emergency, Parliament can legislate on any State List entry. Laws cease 6 months after the emergency ends.
• B-1 (Article 252): State legislature resolutions initiate the process. Only consenting states are bound; others may adopt by subsequent resolution.
• C-4 (Article 249): Triggered by a Rajya Sabha resolution (2/3 of members present and voting), valid for one year (renewable). Law lapses 6 months after resolution expires.
• D-2 (Article 357): During President's Rule, Parliament legislates on State List subjects. These laws survive after President's Rule ends, continuing until the state legislature repeals them — the opposite of Article 250.

Value Addition:
• Article 257 laws under Article 357 survive President's Rule — a unique feature distinguishing it from Article 250.
• S.R. Bommai case scrutinised the validity of the proclamation triggering President's Rule, which in turn validates all legislative action under Article 357.
• Article 249 is the only emergency-free route that requires upper-house (Rajya Sabha) consensus.

solution.concept_anchor: India's residuary power — closer to Canada than USA
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both facts (India's residuary power is with Parliament, and this resembles Canada) may assume R explains A without checking whether the causal link is stated correctly.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? Yes — In India, residuary legislative power vests in Parliament under Article 248 read with Entry 97 of the Union List.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? No — In Canada, residuary power also rests with the Centre (federal Parliament), not with the provinces. So the statement that Canada's residuary power rests with provinces is factually wrong.
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect, the answer must be (c) — A is correct but R is incorrect.
Confirm: correct_option is 'c' — A correct, R incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is a factual inversion in R. Students who know India resembles Canada on residuary power often believe Canada vests residuary power with provinces (like the USA), making them think India is unique. In fact, Canada also vests residuary power with the federal Parliament. The USA is the country that vests it with states. A candidate who has half-knowledge will find R plausible and choose (a) or (b) without verifying R's factual accuracy.
solution.final_explanation:
Residuary legislative power refers to the power to legislate on subjects not enumerated in any of the three lists of the Seventh Schedule. This is tested frequently in comparative constitutional contexts.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: Article 248 read with Entry 97 of the Union List vests residuary legislative power exclusively in Parliament. States have no claim over subjects not covered by any list.
• Reason (R) — Incorrect: R claims Canada's residuary power rests with provinces. This is factually wrong. In Canada, residuary power rests with the federal Parliament (like India), not with the provinces. The USA is the country where residuary power rests with the states (10th Amendment). India's model is closer to Canada, not the USA — but for the reason that BOTH vest residuary power centrally, not because Canada vests it with provinces.

Value Addition:
• USA 10th Amendment: Powers not delegated to the federal government are reserved to the states — residuary with states.
• Canada's Constitution Act 1867: Residuary power with the federal Parliament — same as India.
• The judicial test for identifying a residuary subject is: whether after liberal construction it falls in any existing entry. Only if it does not, does it become residuary.

solution.concept_anchor: 42nd Amendment sequence and list entry reshuffling
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know the 42nd Amendment came before the 44th Amendment may confuse the exact year of the 42nd Amendment (1976) with 1975 or 1978, altering perceived sequence.
elimination_logic: The original Constitution (1950) had Education in the State List — this is the starting point.
The 42nd Amendment (1976) transferred Education, Forests, and Wild Animals from the State List to the Concurrent List — this came next.
The 44th Amendment (1978) deleted Article 257A (which the 42nd Amendment had inserted allowing armed forces deployment without state consent) — this came after.
The 101st Amendment (2016) inserted Article 246A, creating concurrent GST taxing power — the most recent event. Correct chronological order: 1 → 3 → 4 → 2, which corresponds to option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who know only that the 42nd and 44th Amendments are sequenced may not know the precise constitutional change each made, leading to confusion between items 3 and 4 in the sequence. Additionally, confusing Article 257A's deletion (44th Amendment) with other 44th Amendment changes (like restoring 'socialist' and 'secular' to the Preamble) creates sequencing errors.
solution.final_explanation:
Correct order: 1 → 3 → 4 → 2.
• Event 1 (Original Constitution, 1950): Education was a State List subject — the constitutional baseline.
• Event 3 (42nd Amendment, 1976): Education, Forests, Wild Animals, and Weights & Measures transferred to Concurrent List — major centralisation during Emergency.
• Event 4 (44th Amendment, 1978): Article 257A deleted — this provision allowed Central armed forces deployment in states without consent and was inserted by the 42nd Amendment.
• Event 2 (101st Amendment, 2016): Article 246A inserted, creating GST concurrent taxing power outside the three-list framework.

Value Addition:
• The 42nd Amendment is the most wide-ranging amendment, making over 50 changes to the Constitution.
• The 44th Amendment partially reversed Emergency-era centralisations.
• GST under Article 246A is explicitly outside the Union, State, and Concurrent Lists — a unique constitutional position.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 252 — binding nature and state adoption mechanism
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Article 252 requires state consent may assume the non-consenting state has permanent immunity and choose option (b), missing the adoption mechanism.
elimination_logic: The scenario involves Parliament legislating on a State List subject after some states requested it — this is the Article 252 framework.
Eliminate option (a): Parliament does not need a Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 252 — that is Article 249's requirement.
Eliminate option (b): A state that did not originally consent is NOT permanently excluded — it can adopt the law by passing a similar resolution in its legislature.
Eliminate option (c): Article 252 legislation cannot be amended by any individual consenting state; only Parliament can amend it.
Option (d) is correct: The non-consenting State Y can adopt the Parliamentary law by passing a resolution to that effect in its own legislature.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) is the trap — it exploits the reasonable belief that a state that did not consent to Article 252 legislation is permanently unaffected. In reality, such states can voluntarily 'adopt' the law later by their own resolution. The permanent exclusion principle does not exist under Article 252.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 252 enables Parliament to legislate on a State List subject when two or more state legislatures request it. The scenario describes this mechanism and tests its less-known consequences.

Applicable principle: Article 252's adoption mechanism.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Article 252 is triggered by state legislature resolutions, not a Rajya Sabha resolution. The Rajya Sabha resolution route is Article 249.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: State Y's non-participation does not make it permanently immune. Article 252 allows non-consenting states to adopt the law later by passing a similar resolution.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The irrevocability feature under Article 252 means consenting states (X and Z) cannot amend or repeal the law — only Parliament can.
• Option (d) — Correct: State Y can adopt the Parliamentary law by passing a resolution in its own legislature expressing that intent. This is the adoption mechanism explicitly provided under Article 252.

Value Addition:
• The Prize Competition Act 1955 and Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974 are the two most commonly cited Article 252 examples.
• Once a state adopts Article 252 legislation, it too loses the power to amend or repeal it.
• Article 252 represents state-initiated cooperative federalism — contrasting with Article 253's Union-initiated approach.

concepts_used: Doctrine of Pith and Substance in Legislative Entries
Doctrine of Colourable Legislation

solution.concept_anchor: Colourable legislation — applies to competence not fundamental rights
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students may think 'occupied field' is a separate doctrine unrelated to pith and substance and therefore the odd one out, missing that colourable legislation is the one with a different application domain.
elimination_logic: Identify the common category: doctrines used to determine legislative competence over the three lists.
Pith and substance — tests the true nature and character of a law to determine competence. Belongs to the category.
Occupied field — determines whether Parliament has comprehensively covered a concurrent subject, voiding state law. Belongs to the category.

Colourable legislation — is about disguised legislative intent and the maxim 'what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly.' It applies to legislative competence BUT the UPSC trap is that it does NOT apply to fundamental rights violations — making its domain different from the others. Still, it relates to competence.

Harmonious construction — is a rule of statutory/constitutional interpretation used to resolve conflicts between list entries by giving them their widest scope. This is an interpretive tool, not a doctrine of competence review. It is the odd one out among doctrines specifically testing legislative validity.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students may confuse colourable legislation with something unrelated because of the 'indirect' maxim. However, the genuine odd one out is 'harmonious construction' — it is a principle of textual interpretation of list entries, not a doctrine for determining whether a law is validly enacted by the competent legislature. The other three (pith and substance, occupied field, colourable legislation) all deal with whether a legislature had competence to enact a specific law.
solution.final_explanation:
The question groups doctrines from constitutional adjudication of legislative competence disputes.

• Pith and substance: Tests the true nature and character of legislation. If substantially within competence, incidental encroachment on another list is tolerated.
• Occupied field: Tests whether Parliament has comprehensively covered a Concurrent List field, thereby voiding even non-contradictory state legislation.
• Colourable legislation: Applies the maxim 'what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly' — catches disguised encroachment on another legislature's domain.
• Harmonious construction: An interpretive principle directing courts to give entries the widest meaning and avoid conflicts — it does not determine competence of a legislature but guides how list entries are read.

Harmonious construction is the odd one out — it is an interpretive canon, not a validity-testing doctrine.

Value Addition:
• Pith and substance originated in the Privy Council's Cushing v. Dupuy; first applied in India in State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara.
• Colourable legislation doctrine does NOT apply to fundamental rights violations — it is limited to legislative competence.
• GVK Industries v. Union of India is the leading case on harmonious construction of list entries.

(a) Doctrine of pith and substance
(b) Doctrine of occupied field
(c) Doctrine of colourable legislation
(d) Rule of harmonious construction of list entries

GST and Article 246A: Concurrent Taxing Power and Federal Restructuring

solution.concept_anchor: No taxation in Concurrent List — Article 246A outside three-list scheme

statement_analysis.statement: The Concurrent List of the Seventh Schedule contains no entry relating to the imposition of any tax, making taxation a strictly bifurcated subject between the Union and State Lists.
statement_analysis.reason: Taxation is exclusively divided between the Union and State Lists. There are no tax entries in the Concurrent List — this is a defining structural feature of India's fiscal federalism.

statement_analysis.statement: The Goods and Services Tax is levied under the authority of Entry 92C of the Union List, which was inserted by the 101st Constitutional Amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: GST is levied under Article 246A, which was inserted by the 101st Amendment. Entry 92C (taxes on services) was inserted by the 88th Amendment but was never brought into force and was subsumed by GST. Article 246A is outside the three-list scheme — it is not placed in any list.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know GST was created by a constitutional amendment may accept Statement 2 as broadly correct without verifying whether Entry 92C or Article 246A is the actual vehicle.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: No Concurrent List tax entry is a well-established constitutional design principle. Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: Entry 92C (taxes on services) was inserted by the 88th Amendment — NOT the 101st. The 101st Amendment inserted Article 246A for GST, which operates OUTSIDE all three lists. Statement 2 falsely attributes GST's authority to Entry 92C. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Only Statement 1 is correct — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Entry 92C is a genuine constitutional provision (inserted by the 88th Amendment for taxes on services) but was never operationalised and was effectively superseded by GST under Article 246A. A student who remembers '88th Amendment — services tax — Entry 92C' and vaguely associates it with GST will find Statement 2 highly plausible, especially with the authoritative-sounding '101st Amendment' attribution that is real but applied to the wrong provision.
solution.final_explanation:
India's fiscal federalism has a unique structure: taxation is entirely distributed between Union and State Lists, with no tax entry in the Concurrent List.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Concurrent List has no taxation entries. This is structural — taxes have always been assigned exclusively to either Parliament or State Legislatures, creating clear fiscal domains.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: GST authority flows from Article 246A, inserted by the 101st Constitutional Amendment (2016). Article 246A is a standalone provision outside the three-list scheme. Entry 92C (taxes on services) was inserted by the 88th Amendment but was never brought into force and was subsumed by GST.

Value Addition:
• Article 246A(2) gives Parliament alone the power over inter-state supply (IGST) — even within the concurrent GST framework.
• The GST Council (Article 279A) was also a constitutional creation of the 101st Amendment.
• Supreme Court in Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022): GST Council recommendations are persuasive but not binding on Parliament or state legislatures.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 262 — exclusion of Supreme Court jurisdiction over inter-state water disputes
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know that inter-state matters are generally adjudicated by the Supreme Court may instinctively choose option (a), not recalling that Article 262 is one of the rare provisions allowing exclusion of SC jurisdiction.
elimination_logic: The blank concerns the unique constitutional provision relating to inter-state river disputes and judicial jurisdiction.
Eliminate option (a): The Constitution does NOT guarantee Supreme Court jurisdiction over water disputes — Article 262 explicitly allows Parliament to exclude it.
Eliminate option (b): High Courts do not have jurisdiction over inter-state water disputes — these are federal disputes.
Eliminate option (d): A National Water Tribunal is not a constitutional body mentioned in any article.
Option (c) is correct: Article 262 empowers Parliament to provide that neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall exercise jurisdiction over inter-state water disputes.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is in assuming the Supreme Court's jurisdiction is guaranteed over all disputes between states. Article 262 is one of the very few constitutional provisions that explicitly allows Parliament to exclude even the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction. Students who know Article 131 gives the Supreme Court exclusive jurisdiction in federal disputes may assume water disputes follow the same rule.
solution.final_explanation:
Entry 17 of the State List covers water (irrigation, canals, drainage) as an ordinary state subject. Entry 56 of the Union List allows Parliament to regulate inter-state rivers if declared expedient in public interest.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Article 262 does not guarantee Supreme Court jurisdiction — it does the opposite, allowing Parliament to exclude SC jurisdiction.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: High Courts have no jurisdiction over inter-state water disputes; these transcend state boundaries.
• Option (c) — Correct: Article 262 empowers Parliament to exclude Supreme Court (and any other court) jurisdiction over inter-state water disputes — a unique derogation from SC's usual federal adjudicatory role.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: A 'National Water Tribunal' is not a constitutionally named body; the mechanism is a statutory tribunal under the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956.

Value Addition:
• Article 262 is one of very few provisions allowing exclusion of Supreme Court's jurisdiction — frequently tested.
• The 2019 amendment to the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act aimed to create a permanent tribunal structure.
• Article 131 gives SC original jurisdiction over federal disputes — Article 262 carves out an exception for water disputes.

(b) The concerned High Courts shall constitute special benches to resolve inter-state river water disputes
(c) Neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall exercise jurisdiction in respect of any inter-state water dispute
(d) A permanent National Water Tribunal constituted under Article 262 shall be the sole adjudicatory body

concepts_used: Special Provisions for Certain States and Legislative Relations (Articles 371-371J)

solution.concept_anchor: Articles 371A and 371G — asymmetric federal legislative protection
solution.strong_distractor: a — Nagaland's Article 371A protection is the most famous such provision; students who know it may not know Mizoram (371G) has similar protection and may confuse which article number goes with which state.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Article 371A protects Nagaland, not Manipur. Manipur has special provisions under Article 371C but not the same legislative veto power.

Confirm option (b): Article 371G protects Mizo customary law — Parliament cannot make laws on Mizo customary law and practices without the Mizoram State Assembly's resolution. This is correctly matched.
Eliminate option (c): Article 371D relates to Andhra Pradesh/Telangana — it concerns public employment and educational opportunities, not customary law protection.
Eliminate option (d): Arunachal Pradesh does not have a provision identical to Articles 371A or 371G regarding customary law legislative veto.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who know Nagaland has special legislative protection (Article 371A) may confuse it with Manipur (option a) because both are North-Eastern states. The entity-swap uses states within the same region. Additionally, Article 371G for Mizoram is less commonly taught than 371A for Nagaland, making option (b) the harder correct answer.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 371A to 371J create asymmetric federalism by giving certain states special protections that override the normal operation of Parliamentary legislative supremacy.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Article 371A protects Nagaland, not Manipur. Manipur is covered under Article 371C, which concerns a Hill Areas Committee, not customary law protection from Parliamentary legislation.
• Option (b) — Correct: Article 371G provides that no Parliamentary law on Mizo customary law and practices shall apply to Mizoram unless the State Assembly passes a resolution to that effect — identical in structure to Article 371A for Nagaland.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Article 371D relates to Andhra Pradesh, concerning equitable opportunities in public employment and education — not customary law.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Arunachal Pradesh does not have a customary law legislative veto equivalent to Articles 371A or 371G.

Value Addition:
• Articles 371A and 371G are the only provisions giving state assemblies a veto over Central legislation on customary law.
• These provisions reflect the unique tribal law traditions recognised during statehood negotiations.
• Such protections are outside the three-list scheme — they function as constitutional overrides.

concepts_used: Centre's Power to Give Directions to States on Legislative/Executive Matters: Articles 256-257

solution.concept_anchor: Article 257A — deleted provision on armed forces deployment

statement_analysis.statement: Article 256 of the Constitution imposes an obligation on state governments to ensure that their executive power does not impede or prejudice the exercise of the executive power of the Union.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 256 precisely places this obligation on states — their executive power must be exercised to ensure compliance with Parliamentary laws and must not conflict with Union executive power.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 257A, which allowed the Union to deploy its armed forces in any state for the maintenance of public order without the state's consent, currently forms part of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 257A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) but was subsequently deleted by the 44th Amendment (1978). It no longer exists as a constitutional provision.

statement_analysis.statement: Non-compliance by a state with Union directions issued under Articles 256 or 257 can constitute a ground for the imposition of President's Rule under Article 356.
statement_analysis.reason: Failure of a state to comply with Union directions under Articles 256-257 is explicitly one of the grounds on which President's Rule can be imposed — it is a constitutional consequence of non-compliance.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Article 257A existed during the Emergency era may believe it is still part of the Constitution, treating Statement 2 as correct and incorrectly selecting an option that excludes it.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: Article 256 does impose exactly this obligation on states — executive power must not impede Parliament's laws. Statement 1 is correct (not incorrect).
Check Statement 2: Article 257A was deleted by the 44th Amendment — it does not currently exist. Statement 2 IS incorrect.
Check Statement 3: Non-compliance with Union directions under Articles 256-257 is a ground for Article 356 President's Rule. Statement 3 is correct (not incorrect).
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct — answer is (b): 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Article 257A is a deleted provision that many students treat as still operative, especially because its topic (Central deployment of armed forces in states) remains a live political issue. The question exploits this by asking which statements are NOT correct, making students who believe 257A still exists incorrectly treat Statement 2 as a correct statement. The 44th Amendment's deletion of 257A was a deliberate reversal of Emergency-era centralisation.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 256-257 form the executive compliance framework of Centre-State relations, supplementing the legislative distribution of the Seventh Schedule.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 256 obligates state executive power to comply with Parliamentary laws and not impede Union executive power. This is not incorrect.
• Statement 2 — NOT Correct: Article 257A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment to allow Central armed forces deployment in states without state consent, was deleted by the 44th Amendment (1978). Any current question about such deployment cannot invoke Article 257A — it no longer exists.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 356 can be invoked when a state fails to carry on government in accordance with the Constitution, which includes failure to comply with Union directions under Articles 256-257. This is not incorrect.

Value Addition:
• The 44th Amendment reversed several Emergency-era constitutional changes made by the 42nd Amendment.
• Article 257 allows the Union to give directions to states on protecting railways and nationally/militarily important communications.
• The Inter-State Council under Article 263 is the recommended forum for resolving such Centre-State executive compliance disputes.

concepts_used: Doctrine of Pith and Substance in Legislative Entries

solution.concept_anchor: Pith and substance origin — Privy Council and Indian application
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know pith and substance is used for legislative competence disputes may conflate it with the colourable legislation doctrine, which also deals with competence but focuses on disguised intent rather than incidental encroachment.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Colourable legislation addresses disguised intent ('what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly') — distinct from pith and substance which tests bona fide but incidentally overlapping legislation.
Eliminate option (b): Harmonious construction is an interpretive rule for reading list entries broadly — it does not determine legislative validity or resolve competence disputes directly.
Option (c) correctly states pith and substance: a law valid if its true nature and character falls within the legislating body's competence, even if it incidentally encroaches on another list.
Eliminate option (d): 'Occupied field' concerns comprehensive Parliamentary coverage of a Concurrent List subject — a different doctrine with different application.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Options (a) and (c) are frequently conflated because both deal with legislative competence. The difference: colourable legislation tests whether the legislature is disguising its true purpose (mala fide); pith and substance tests whether the true subject matter is within competence regardless of incidental effects. A student who knows both doctrines but imprecisely may choose (a) by confusing 'true nature' with 'disguised intent.'
solution.final_explanation:
The doctrine of pith and substance is the primary tool for resolving legislative competence disputes between the Union and states.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: This describes the colourable legislation doctrine. Colourable legislation focuses on whether a legislature is indirectly doing what it cannot do directly — a mala fide or disguised encroachment test.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Harmonious construction directs courts to give list entries the widest meaning to avoid conflicts — it is an interpretive principle, not a competence-testing doctrine.
• Option (c) — Correct: Pith and substance holds that if a law's true nature and character falls within the legislating body's competence, the law is valid even if it incidentally trenches on another list's entries. First applied in India in State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Occupied field doctrine addresses Parliamentary intent to comprehensively cover a Concurrent subject — applicable to Centre-State concurrent field conflicts, not the general competence test.

Value Addition:
• The Privy Council in Cushing v. Dupuy first articulated pith and substance.
• The doctrine applies more to Union-State List conflicts than to Concurrent List conflicts.
• It cannot save legislation that is substantially (not just incidentally) outside legislative competence.

formatted_presentation.display_text:

(a) A legislature cannot achieve indirectly what it is constitutionally prohibited from doing directly, and courts will look through the form to identify the true legislative purpose
(b) List entries must be given the widest possible construction to avoid conflicts between Union and State legislative powers, preferring interpretations that uphold validity
(c) A law is constitutionally valid if its true nature and character falls within the legislating body's competence, even if it incidentally trenches upon subjects assigned to another list
(d) Once Parliament has comprehensively occupied a field in the Concurrent List, any State legislation on the same subject is void even in the absence of direct conflict

concepts_used: Sarkaria and Punchhi Commission Recommendations on Legislative Relations

solution.concept_anchor: Sarkaria vs Punchhi Commission — distinct recommendations

statement_analysis.statement: The Sarkaria Commission (1983) recommended that Article 249 should be used sparingly and only in cases of genuine national necessity, with prior consultation with affected states.
statement_analysis.reason: Sarkaria Commission explicitly recommended restrained use of Article 249 and emphasised prior consultation with states before Parliament legislates on State List subjects in the name of national interest.

statement_analysis.statement: The Punchhi Commission (2007) introduced the concept of a 'localisation principle' for the Concurrent List, recommending that subjects of primarily local importance within the Concurrent List be transferred back to the State List.
statement_analysis.reason: The Punchhi Commission recommended a 'localisation principle' — subjects whose administration is predominantly local in character should be transferred from the Concurrent List to the State List to strengthen state autonomy.

statement_analysis.statement: Both the Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions recommended abolishing the Inter-State Council under Article 263 as an ineffective mechanism for Centre-State legislative coordination.
statement_analysis.reason: Both commissions actually recommended STRENGTHENING the Inter-State Council under Article 263 and using it as the primary forum for Centre-State coordination — neither recommended its abolition.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who vaguely know that both commissions were critical of existing Centre-State mechanisms may assume they recommended abolishing the Inter-State Council, making all three statements seem correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Sarkaria Commission's recommendation on Article 249 (sparingly, with state consultation) is accurate. Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2: Punchhi Commission's 'localisation principle' for Concurrent List is a specific and accurate recommendation. Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 3: Both commissions recommended STRENGTHENING, not abolishing, the Inter-State Council. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Only Statements 1 and 2 are correct — answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the trap. Students who know both commissions were critical of Centre-State relations and recommended reforms may assume 'reform' extended to abolishing ineffective institutions. In reality, both commissions wanted to revive and strengthen the Inter-State Council — recognising it as underutilised rather than structurally flawed. The entity-swap trap is between 'abolishing' and 'strengthening.'
solution.final_explanation:
The Sarkaria Commission (1983) and Punchhi Commission (2007) are the two major executive commissions on Centre-State relations, frequently tested in both Prelims and Mains.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Sarkaria Commission recommended that Article 249 (National Interest legislation on State List) should be invoked sparingly, with genuine national necessity, and that states should be consulted beforehand.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Punchhi Commission introduced the 'localisation principle' — subjects in the Concurrent List that are primarily local in character should be returned to the State List to restore state autonomy.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Both commissions recommended making the Inter-State Council under Article 263 MORE effective and using it as the primary forum for Centre-State legislative coordination — the opposite of abolition.

Value Addition:
• Sarkaria Commission: Set up in 1983; submitted report in 1988 — the delay itself is notable.
• Punchhi Commission: Set up in 2007; submitted report in 2010 with 273 recommendations.
• Neither commission's recommendations are legally binding — implementation depends entirely on political will.
• Inter-State Council was finally constituted in 1990, over 40 years after the Constitution came into force.

concepts_used: Doctrine of Occupied Field in Concurrent List Legislation

solution.concept_anchor: Occupied field doctrine — voids state law without direct conflict
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who correctly identify both A and R as factually true may not carefully evaluate whether R causally explains A, accepting the relationship without scrutiny.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? Yes — The occupied field doctrine can void a State law even without any direct contradiction with Central law, as established in Zaverbhai Amaidas v. State of Bombay.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? Yes — Parliament's intent to comprehensively cover a legislative field is indeed the operative basis for the occupied field doctrine, distinguishing it from simple repugnancy.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? Yes — The reason a State law is void without direct contradiction is precisely because Parliament's comprehensive coverage signals legislative intent to occupy the field completely, leaving no room for state legislation. R is the direct causal explanation for A.
Both A and R correct, R explains A — correct option is (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The occupied field doctrine is a nuanced extension of the repugnancy principle under Article 254, operating on the Concurrent List.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: A State law on a Concurrent List subject can be rendered void even if it does not directly contradict any provision of a Central law. This is the counter-intuitive but judicially settled 'occupied field' principle — established in Zaverbhai Amaidas v. State of Bombay.
• Reason (R) — Correct: Parliament's intent to comprehensively cover the field is what activates the occupied field doctrine. When Parliament intends its legislation to be exhaustive and complete, there is simply no legislative room left for state legislation on the same subject.
• Causal relationship: R correctly and causally explains A. The State law is void (A) because Parliament has signalled — through comprehensive coverage — an intent to occupy the field completely (R), leaving no space for supplementary state law even without direct conflict.

Value Addition:
• Contrast: Direct repugnancy requires provision-by-provision contradiction; occupied field requires only inferred Parliamentary intent to be exhaustive.
• Courts distinguish between 'intentional lacunae' (Parliament left gaps deliberately — state can fill) and 'occupied field' (Parliament covered comprehensively — no room for states).
• The doctrine applies only to Concurrent List subjects, not to Union or State List subjects.

formatted_presentation.display_text:
Assertion (A): Under the doctrine of occupied field, a State law on a Concurrent List subject may be rendered void by a Central law even when no provision of the State law directly contradicts any provision of the Central law.

Reason (R): The operative basis of the occupied field doctrine is Parliament's intent to comprehensively cover the legislative field, leaving no room for State legislation on the same subject regardless of the absence of direct conflict.

(a) Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
(b) Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(c) A is correct but R is incorrect
(d) A is incorrect but R is correct

concepts_used: GST and Article 246A: Concurrent Taxing Power and Federal Restructuring

solution.concept_anchor: Article 246A — GST federal structure and GST Council binding force

statement_analysis.statement: Article 246A grants both Parliament and State Legislatures the power to make laws with respect to Goods and Services Tax.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 246A (inserted by the 101st Amendment) explicitly grants concurrent power to both Parliament and State Legislatures to legislate on GST — a constitutional departure from the exclusive lists model.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 246A, Parliament has exclusive power over the GST on inter-state supply of goods and services (IGST), which no State Legislature can legislate on.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 246A(2) specifically reserves to Parliament alone the power to make laws on inter-state supply of goods or services — IGST is exclusively Parliamentary.

statement_analysis.statement: The GST Council established under Article 279A is a constitutional body whose recommendations are legally binding on both Parliament and the State Legislatures.
statement_analysis.reason: The Supreme Court in Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022) held that GST Council recommendations are persuasive but not legally binding — Parliament and state legislatures retain the freedom to deviate from GST Council recommendations.

statement_analysis.statement: The 101st Constitutional Amendment modified entries in both the Union List and the State List to accommodate the GST framework.
statement_analysis.reason: The 101st Amendment modified Entry 84 of the Union List (removing tobacco, petroleum products) and Entry 54 of the State List (removing these from state tax domain) — structural changes to align the existing lists with the GST architecture.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know GST Council is a constitutional body created by Article 279A may assume its recommendations are automatically binding, failing to register the Mohit Minerals ruling.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — Article 246A explicitly grants concurrent GST power to both Parliament and states.
Statement 2 is correct — Article 246A(2) reserves IGST exclusively for Parliament.
Statement 3 is incorrect — GST Council recommendations are persuasive, not binding (Mohit Minerals, 2022). Being a constitutional body does not make recommendations binding.
Statement 4 is correct — 101st Amendment modified Entries 84 (Union) and 54 (State) among others.
Three statements (1, 2, 4) are correct — answer is (c) Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the key trap. Being a 'constitutional body' is often conflated with having 'binding authority.' The GST Council is indeed established by Article 279A (constitutional status), but the Supreme Court in Mohit Minerals (2022) clarified that its recommendations are only persuasive, not binding. Students who equate constitutional status with binding decisions will mark Statement 3 as correct and choose (d).
solution.final_explanation:
Article 246A (101st Amendment, 2016) and Article 279A together restructured India's fiscal federalism for the GST era.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 246A creates a concurrent taxing power for GST — both Parliament and state legislatures can legislate on GST, marking a constitutional break from the exclusive list model.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The proviso to Article 246A(2) reserves inter-state supply (IGST) exclusively for Parliament — states cannot legislate on cross-border transactions.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Supreme Court in Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022) categorically held that GST Council recommendations are persuasive but not legally binding. Parliament and state legislatures may deviate from them within constitutional limits.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The 101st Amendment modified Union List Entry 84 (excise duty — excluding petroleum, tobacco) and State List Entry 54 (sales tax) to align with the GST structure.

Value Addition:
• GST Council requires a three-fourth weighted majority for decisions — Centre has 1/3 vote, all states together have 2/3.
• Article 246A is outside the three-list scheme of the Seventh Schedule — it is a standalone concurrent power.
• States surrendered exclusive tax rights on goods; Centre surrendered exclusive rights on services — a cooperative federal bargain.

concepts_used: Doctrine of Colourable Legislation

solution.concept_anchor: Colourable legislation — applies to competence not fundamental rights violation
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students may confuse colourable legislation with a fundamental rights violation challenge, especially when the scenario involves a state taking property — invoking Article 300A instinctively.
elimination_logic: The scenario involves a legislature enacting a law that appears to be in one domain but is actually designed to encroach on another legislature's exclusive domain — this is the colourable legislation fact pattern.
Eliminate option (a): Colourable legislation doctrine does NOT apply to fundamental rights violations — its domain is legislative competence only. This is the classic UPSC trap on this doctrine.
Eliminate option (b): Pith and substance tests bona fide incidental encroachment — it would help the state, not invalidate the law for disguised intent.
Eliminate option (c): Harmonious construction is used to reconcile list entries — not to catch disguised legislative intent.

Option (d) is correct: The colourable legislation doctrine applies when a legislature does indirectly what it cannot do directly — the State here is disguising a regulation of banking (Union subject) as a consumer protection law (Concurrent subject).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The UPSC trap annotation in the key dimensions is directly exploited here: colourable legislation applies to legislative competence, NOT to fundamental rights violations. Option (a) tempts students who associate state action against a business with a rights challenge under Article 300A (right to property) or Article 19(1)(g). The scenario is designed to make the rights framing seem natural, but the correct legal challenge is competence-based.
solution.final_explanation:
The colourable legislation doctrine applies the maxim 'what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly' to legislative competence disputes.

Applicable principle: A State legislature cannot use a Concurrent List subject (consumer protection) as a vehicle to regulate a Union List subject (banking regulation) — if that is the true purpose, the law is colourable.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Colourable legislation is exclusively a legislative competence doctrine. It does NOT apply to challenges based on fundamental rights violations. Confusing the two is the primary trap here.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Pith and substance would be invoked to defend the law (testing whether its true character is consumer protection). It is not the doctrine that captures disguised encroachment.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Harmonious construction reconciles overlapping entries — it does not address a legislature's mala fide or disguised legislative intent.
• Option (d) — Correct: Colourable legislation (K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa) captures situations where a legislature disguises the true purpose of legislation to encroach on another legislature's exclusive domain.

Value Addition:
• K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo: Orissa Estates Abolition Act — benchmark colourable legislation case.
• The doctrine is sometimes described as the 'fraud on the Constitution' principle.
• Courts look at the practical effect and true purpose of the law, not its stated classification.

(b) The doctrine of pith and substance, which would test whether the law's true character relates to banking or consumer protection

concepts_used: Structure and Composition of the Three Lists (Seventh Schedule)
42nd Amendment (1976): Redistribution of Legislative Entries

solution.concept_anchor: Current entry counts — Union 100, State 61, Concurrent 52

statement_analysis.statement: The Union List currently contains 100 entries.
statement_analysis.reason: The current Union List has 100 entries — this is the post-amendment count that students must know, distinct from the original count.

statement_analysis.statement: The State List currently contains 66 entries, the same as in the original Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: The State List currently contains 61 entries. The 42nd Amendment (1976) transferred several subjects (Education, Forests, Weights & Measures, Wild Animals) from the State List to the Concurrent List, reducing its count.

statement_analysis.statement: The Concurrent List currently contains 52 entries.
statement_analysis.reason: The current Concurrent List has 52 entries — expanded from the original 47 entries by the 42nd Amendment which added transferred State List subjects.

statement_analysis.statement: The original Constitution had 97 entries in the Union List, but this was later increased through successive amendments.
statement_analysis.reason: The original Union List had 97 entries (not 97 — actually the original count was 97 entries). The 42nd Amendment and other amendments changed the numbering, resulting in the current count of 100. However, saying it was 'later increased through successive amendments' oversimplifies — entries were also deleted, and renumbered. More precisely, the original count was 97 and current is 100, but the mechanism involved both additions and deletions.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who remember '97 entries in Union List' (the original count) and '66 entries in State List' (an approximated wrong number) will find options aligning with three correct statements.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Union List = 100 entries (current). Correct.
Statement 2: State List = 61 entries (current), NOT 66. The 42nd Amendment reduced the State List. Statement 2 is incorrect — it states 66 and claims no change.
Statement 3: Concurrent List = 52 entries (current). Correct.

Statement 4: Original Union List had 97 entries — but the statement claims increases through 'successive amendments' which is oversimplified and contains the specific error of implying the original was 97 and it only went up. Some entries were deleted, some added — the statement mischaracterises the process. Statement 4 is incorrect.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — answer is (b) Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the primary trap, exploiting the most common UPSC trap annotated in the key dimensions — students who have memorised approximate or pre-amendment numbers. The number '66' for the State List sounds plausible and is in the vicinity of the correct figure (61), causing students who are not precise to treat it as correct. Similarly, Statement 4's claim about the Union List's original count is broadly directionally true but contains the misleading implication of only upward movement.
solution.final_explanation:
The entry counts in the three lists are a high-frequency factual test and a common UPSC trap.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The current Union List has 100 entries.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The current State List has 61 entries, not 66. The 42nd Amendment (1976) transferred Education, Forests, Wild Animals, and Weights & Measures from the State List to the Concurrent List, reducing the count from the original.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The current Concurrent List has 52 entries, expanded from the original 47 by the 42nd Amendment's transfers from the State List.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The characterisation of only 'successive increases' in the Union List is misleading. While the current count of 100 is higher than the original, entries have been both added and deleted over time; the 101st Amendment, for instance, deleted some entries in connection with GST.

Value Addition:
• Memory aid: 100-61-52 (Union-State-Concurrent) — current counts.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 250 — Parliament's power and post-emergency sunset

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 250, Parliament acquires the power to legislate on any entry in the State List while a Proclamation of National Emergency is in operation, without requiring any Rajya Sabha resolution or state consent.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 250's scope extends to ANY State List entry during National Emergency, and is triggered solely by the Presidential Proclamation under Article 352 — no Rajya Sabha resolution or state consent is needed.

statement_analysis.statement: A law enacted by Parliament under Article 250 remains operative indefinitely after the National Emergency ceases, unless Parliament itself repeals it.
statement_analysis.reason: Laws enacted under Article 250 cease to operate 6 months after the Proclamation of National Emergency ceases — they do not survive indefinitely. This is the explicit sunset clause differentiating Article 250 from Article 357.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Article 250 exists and broadly know Parliament can legislate on State List during emergency may accept both statements as broadly correct without registering the critical 6-month sunset clause.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 250 is triggered by Presidential proclamation alone (Article 352 in force) — no Rajya Sabha resolution needed (that's Article 249). Parliament can legislate on ANY State List entry. Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Article 250 laws have an explicit 6-month sunset after the emergency ceases — they do NOT remain operative indefinitely. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits confusion between Article 250 and Article 357. Laws under Article 357 (President's Rule) DO survive after the emergency ends. Laws under Article 250 (National Emergency) lapse 6 months after the emergency ceases. Students who know one provision's rules but confuse them across articles will mark Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 250 dramatically expands Parliamentary legislative competence during National Emergency, but with important temporal limitations.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 250 gives Parliament the power to legislate on ANY entry in the State List while a National Emergency under Article 352 is in force. The trigger is the Presidential Proclamation alone — no Rajya Sabha resolution (that is Article 249's requirement) and no state consent (that is Article 252's feature) are needed.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 250 contains an explicit sunset clause. Laws made under it cease to operate 6 months after the National Emergency ceases. They do not survive indefinitely. This is a key distinguishing feature from Article 357 (President's Rule) laws, which do survive after President's Rule ends unless the state legislature repeals them.

Value Addition:
• During National Emergency: State laws on the subject are not repealed — Parliamentary law prevails; state law revives after emergency ceases.
• The 6-month post-emergency survival window allows an orderly transition back to state legislative authority.
• Article 250 was relevant during the 1962 (India-China), 1965 (India-Pakistan), and 1971 wars and the 1975 Internal Emergency.

solution.concept_anchor: List hierarchy — Union > Concurrent > State in genuine overlap
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know the Concurrent List is shared between Union and States may instinctively place it highest in hierarchy, forgetting Union List supremacy.
elimination_logic: The blank asks for the order of precedence when a genuine legislative overlap cannot be resolved by harmonious construction alone.
Eliminate option (a): State List does not have precedence over either the Union or Concurrent List in any hierarchy — it is the last in priority.

Confirm option (b): Union List > Concurrent List > State List — in cases of genuine overlap, higher-numbered list (in terms of Union priority) prevails. Parliament's legislative competence on the Union List is supreme.
Eliminate option (c): Concurrent List is not at the top — Union List is. Placing Concurrent List above Union List is the plausible fabrication.
Eliminate option (d): Equal weight among all lists is not the constitutional design — the hierarchy exists precisely to resolve conflicts.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) places the Concurrent List at the top, which sounds plausible to students who associate 'concurrent' with 'shared central authority' and mistakenly believe shared Union-State power ranks higher than Union-exclusive power. The actual hierarchy is Union > Concurrent > State, and this question forces precision on that point.
solution.final_explanation:
When two legislative entries genuinely overlap and harmonious construction cannot fully resolve the conflict, courts apply a hierarchical preference among the three lists.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: State List entries are at the bottom of the hierarchy. State legislative power yields to both Union and Concurrent List entries in the event of genuine overlap.
• Option (b) — Correct: The hierarchy is Union List > Concurrent List > State List. Parliament's exclusive Union List powers rank highest; Concurrent List powers (shared but with Parliamentary supremacy) rank second; State List powers rank last.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Concurrent List is not superior to the Union List. Parliament shares Concurrent List power with states, but its exclusive Union List power is supreme.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Equal weight for all three lists contradicts the structural design. The hierarchy resolves genuine conflicts.

Value Addition:
• The hierarchy applies only when harmonious construction fails to resolve an overlap — courts prefer harmonious reading first.
• GVK Industries v. Union of India affirmed that entries should be construed to avoid constitutional conflict before invoking hierarchy.
• Residuary power (Entry 97, Union List) is the final safety net for subjects falling in no list.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 357 — legislative delegation and post-President's Rule survival

statement_analysis.statement: During President's Rule in a state, Parliament can confer on the President the power to make laws on State List subjects for that state, and the President may further delegate this power to any other authority.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 357(1) expressly permits Parliament to confer legislative power on the President, who may in turn delegate to any authority — an explicit exception to the general non-delegation doctrine in the legislative sphere.

statement_analysis.statement: Laws made by Parliament or by the President under Article 357 cease to operate automatically six months after the President's Rule ends, mirroring the sunset clause under Article 250.
statement_analysis.reason: Unlike Article 250, laws made under Article 357 during President's Rule continue to operate after President's Rule ends. They remain operative until the state legislature repeals or amends them — they do not carry a six-month sunset clause.

statement_analysis.statement: The S.R. Bommai case is relevant to Article 357 because it established that the validity of all legislative action taken during President's Rule depends on the validity of the proclamation imposing President's Rule.
statement_analysis.reason: The Bommai case (1994) held that the President's Rule proclamation is subject to judicial review, and if the proclamation is invalid, all consequential legislative action under Articles 356 and 357 would also be invalid.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 as correct may also accept Statement 2 as correct by applying the Article 250 sunset rule (6 months) to Article 357 — a common cross-article conflation.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Article 357(1) allows Parliament to confer law-making power on the President and permits delegation — correct and well-established.

Statement 2: Article 357 laws survive after President's Rule ends and continue until the state legislature acts — the 6-month sunset is Article 250's rule, NOT Article 357's. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3: Bommai case — judicial review of proclamation validity flows through to all action taken under it. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct — answer is (b): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the most common inter-article confusion in this sub-topic. Article 250 has an explicit 6-month sunset; Article 357 has no such sunset — laws survive. A student who has memorised '6 months' in the context of emergency-related legislation will apply it indiscriminately across Articles 250, 249, and 357, all of which have different post-emergency timelines.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 357 governs the legislative consequences of President's Rule under Article 356 and has features that significantly differ from other emergency legislative powers.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Under Article 357(1), Parliament may confer on the President the power to legislate on State List subjects during President's Rule. The President may further delegate this to any authority — an exception to the non-delegation doctrine, explicitly permitted by the Constitution.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Laws made under Article 357 do NOT carry a 6-month sunset. They continue to operate after President's Rule ends and remain in force until the state legislature — once restored — repeals or amends them. This is the key distinction from Article 250 (National Emergency) laws, which lapse 6 months after the emergency ceases.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Bommai case (1994) established judicial reviewability of the Article 356 proclamation. Since all Article 357 legislative power flows from a valid Article 356 proclamation, an invalid proclamation would invalidate the legislative actions taken under it.

Value Addition:
• Article 357 is a significant exception to the general legislative non-delegation rule recognised in Indian constitutional law.
• Post-President's Rule survival of Article 357 laws can have significant practical consequences for states resuming self-governance.
• S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) is the landmark nine-judge bench decision on Article 356.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 254 — repugnancy tests and M. Karunanidhi case
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know M. Karunanidhi relates to Article 254 may incorrectly assign it to the 'direct conflict test' alone, not knowing it established both tests.
elimination_logic: Match A (Direct conflict test): This test voids a State law where its specific provisions directly contradict Central law provisions — matches description 3.
Match B (Occupied field test): Parliament has comprehensively covered the field with intent to be exhaustive — voids State law even without direct contradiction — matches description 1.
Match C (Article 254(2) Presidential assent): Saves State law on Concurrent subject from repugnancy when Presidential assent is obtained — matches description 4.

Match D (M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India): The Supreme Court case that established both the direct conflict test and occupied field test as the two-pronged repugnancy test — matches description 2. Correct combination: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 → option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is in swapping M. Karunanidhi (which established BOTH tests) with Zaverbhai Amaidas (which is specifically associated with the occupied field doctrine). Students who have studied Zaverbhai Amaidas for the occupied field test may incorrectly assign M. Karunanidhi to description 1 (occupied field only) and swap A and B pairings.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 254 governs repugnancy between Central and State laws on the Concurrent List, and the judicial framework for testing repugnancy was established in M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India.

• A-3 (Direct conflict test): A State law provision that directly contradicts a Central law provision is void to the extent of repugnancy — the most straightforward form of repugnancy.
• B-1 (Occupied field test): Parliament's comprehensive coverage of a field signals intent to occupy it completely — a State law is void even without direct contradiction if Parliament has so occupied the field.
• C-4 (Article 254(2)): Presidential assent to a State Concurrent List law allows it to prevail over prior Central law — but Parliament can subsequently override it.
• D-2 (M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India): This landmark case established BOTH the direct conflict test AND the occupied field test as the two limbs of the Article 254 repugnancy doctrine.

Value Addition:
• Zaverbhai Amaidas v. State of Bombay is specifically associated with the occupied field test in the context of essential commodities.
• Repugnancy voids State law only 'to the extent' of repugnancy — the rest survives.
• Article 254 applies ONLY to Concurrent List — not to situations where states try to legislate on Union List subjects (that's a competence issue).

solution.concept_anchor: Article 249 peacetime nature — no emergency required
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who associate Parliamentary expansion of legislative power with emergency situations may instinctively link Article 249 to some form of emergency, choosing (b).
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): A 2/3 majority of TOTAL Rajya Sabha membership is incorrect — it is 2/3 of members present and voting. Additionally, the statement about National Emergency is wrong.
Eliminate option (b): Article 249 is a PEACETIME provision — it requires no emergency. Linking it to any emergency is a fundamental error.
Eliminate option (c): Article 249 covers State List subjects, not Concurrent List subjects. Parliament already has power over Concurrent List subjects — Article 249 would be superfluous there.

Option (d) is correct: Article 249 is a peacetime provision operative without any emergency, triggered only by a Rajya Sabha resolution (2/3 of members present and voting), giving Parliament power to legislate on State List subjects named in the resolution.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The UPSC-annotated trap here is the confusion between Article 249 (peacetime, Rajya Sabha resolution) and Article 250 (National Emergency, Presidential proclamation). Option (b) conflates these two provisions. Students who have studied emergency provisions first and then Article 249 may incorrectly associate Article 249 with emergency conditions.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 249 is one of the most important peacetime Centre-State legislative provisions, frequently conflated with emergency-based expansions of Parliamentary power.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Two errors — the majority required is 2/3 of members present and voting (not total membership), and Article 249 has nothing to do with National Emergency.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Article 249 operates in peacetime — it requires no national emergency of any kind. This is its most important distinguishing feature from Article 250.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Article 249 applies to State List subjects — Parliament already has power over the Concurrent List and needs no Article 249 resolution for that purpose.
• Option (d) — Correct: Article 249 is a peacetime provision triggered solely by a Rajya Sabha resolution supported by 2/3 of members present and voting, enabling Parliament to legislate on specific State List subjects named in the resolution.

Value Addition:
• Resolution under Article 249 is valid for 1 year, renewable indefinitely through fresh resolutions.
• Law under Article 249 ceases to have effect 6 months after the resolution lapses.
• Unlike Article 250, state legislatures retain concurrent power to legislate during the Article 249 resolution period.
