solution.concept_anchor: Residuary power Article 248 — judicial test and GST outside lists

statement_analysis.statement: Article 248 read with Entry 97 of the Union List vests residuary legislative power exclusively in Parliament, covering all matters not enumerated in any of the three lists.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the precise constitutional basis of residuary power — Article 248 is the operative article, and Entry 97 of the Union List is the entry that captures residuary subjects, giving Parliament exclusive power over them.

statement_analysis.statement: The judicial test for determining whether a subject is 'residuary' requires courts to first check whether the subject falls within any existing list entry after giving those entries their narrowest possible construction.
statement_analysis.reason: The judicial test requires liberal construction of existing entries — if after liberal construction the subject does not fall in any list, it becomes residuary. Narrow construction is the opposite of the correct approach.

statement_analysis.statement: GST under Article 246A operates outside the three-list scheme of the Seventh Schedule and is not placed within Entry 97 of the Union List despite being a subject not covered by any other list entry.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 246A is a standalone constitutional provision inserted by the 101st Amendment — GST authority flows from it directly, not from Entry 97. It is not classified as a residuary subject but as a constitutionally created concurrent taxing power.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know the residuary power test involves 'checking existing entries' may not register that the entries must be liberally (not narrowly) construed, treating Statement 2 as correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Article 248 + Entry 97 = residuary power exclusively in Parliament. Standard and correct.
Statement 2: Judicial test requires LIBERAL construction of existing entries before treating a subject as residuary. 'Narrowest possible construction' is the opposite. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3: Article 246A is outside all three lists — GST is not a residuary subject under Entry 97 but a separately created concurrent power. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's trap is subtle — it correctly describes 'checking existing entries' (which is part of the process) but reverses the construction standard from 'liberal' to 'narrow.' A student who half-remembers the judicial test will focus on the 'checking entries' part and miss the critical construction standard, marking Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Residuary legislative power and its constitutional basis are high-frequency UPSC topics, especially when paired with GST.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 248 is the operative constitutional provision; Entry 97 of the Union List is its Seventh Schedule expression. Together, they vest in Parliament exclusive power over all subjects not in any list.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The judicial test for identifying residuary subjects requires liberal (not narrow) construction of existing entries. Only if a subject cannot be brought within any entry after liberal construction does it qualify as residuary. Narrow construction would expand residuary power inappropriately.
• Statement 3 — Correct: GST under Article 246A is a sui generis constitutional creation — it is not placed in any of the three lists and does not derive authority from Entry 97. It was created outside the Seventh Schedule framework by the 101st Amendment.

Value Addition:
• India's residuary power model resembles Canada's — both vest it centrally. The USA vests residuary power with states (10th Amendment).
• Entry 97 also covers 'any other matter not enumerated in Lists II or III including any tax not mentioned in either of those lists.'
• Courts apply the 'pith and substance' test before resorting to residuary classification — residuary is the last option.

Doctrine of Pith and Substance in Legislative Entries

solution.concept_anchor: Pith and substance vs colourable legislation — distinct doctrines
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both doctrines deal with legislative competence may assume R causally explains A without checking whether pith and substance and colourable legislation actually serve the same function as stated.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? Yes — Pith and substance tests the true nature and character of legislation for competence purposes; colourable legislation tests disguised/mala fide encroachment. They are distinct doctrines.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? No — R states that colourable legislation 'extends' pith and substance. This is factually wrong. Colourable legislation is an independent doctrine applying the maxim 'what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly.' It does NOT extend pith and substance — they operate on different bases (bona fide incidental encroachment vs. disguised intent).
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect, the answer is (c) — A correct, R incorrect.
Confirm: correct_option is 'c'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in R is characterising colourable legislation as an 'extension' of pith and substance. Both relate to legislative competence, but pith and substance operates where the legislature has acted bona fide but its law incidentally encroaches on another domain. Colourable legislation operates where the legislature has mala fide or disguised intent to encroach. Calling one an 'extension' of the other conflates their conceptual bases — option (a) captures students who know both doctrines but imprecisely.
solution.final_explanation:
Assertion (A) and Reason (R) both touch on legislative competence doctrines, but R contains a critical factual error about the relationship between the two doctrines.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: Pith and substance examines whether the true nature and character of a law falls within the legislating body's competence, tolerating incidental encroachments. Colourable legislation tests whether a legislature is disguising its true purpose to encroach on another domain. These are independent, distinct doctrines.
• Reason (R) — Incorrect: R characterises colourable legislation as extending the pith and substance doctrine. This is wrong. Colourable legislation derives from the independent maxim 'what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly' (K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo). It does not build on or extend pith and substance — it operates on a different conceptual basis (mala fide/disguised intent vs. bona fide incidental encroachment).
• Answer: (c) — A is correct, R is incorrect.

Value Addition:
• Pith and substance: Privy Council in Cushing v. Dupuy; Indian application in F.N. Balsara.
• Colourable legislation: Indian Supreme Court in K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa.
• Critical UPSC distinction: Colourable legislation applies to legislative competence only — NOT to fundamental rights violations.

Reason (R): The doctrine of colourable legislation is an extension of the pith and substance doctrine — both test the true subject matter of a law, and a finding of colourable legislation is simply a stronger form of finding that a law's pith and substance falls outside legislative competence.

(b) Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

solution.concept_anchor: Article 253 — unilateral treaty implementation power over State List

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 253, Parliament has the power to make laws implementing any treaty, agreement, or convention with any other country, even if the subject matter falls within the State List.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 253 expressly grants Parliament this power without any qualification about which list the subject falls in — it can override State List exclusivity to implement international obligations.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 253 is limited in its application to treaties with foreign countries and does not cover conventions adopted by international organisations such as the United Nations.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 253 explicitly covers 'treaties, agreements, and conventions with any other country or countries, or decisions made at any international conference, association or other body.' It is not limited to bilateral treaties — decisions of international organisations and multilateral conventions are covered.

statement_analysis.statement: No prior consent of state governments is required for Parliament to enact legislation under Article 253 implementing international obligations touching on State List subjects.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 253 is a unilateral Union power — no state consent is required. This is its key centralising feature, contrasting sharply with Article 252 which requires state legislature resolutions.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Article 253 covers treaties may believe it is limited to bilateral treaties and not multilateral conventions/decisions of international bodies, treating Statement 2 as correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Article 253's scope covers State List subjects — this is its most significant feature. Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2: Article 253 explicitly covers treaties, agreements, conventions AND decisions at international conferences/organisations — not limited to bilateral treaties. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3: No state consent required under Article 253 — it is a unilateral Union power. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct — answer is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits a common assumption that 'treaty' means only bilateral treaties between two countries. Article 253 explicitly includes 'decisions made at any international conference, association or other body' — covering UN conventions, WTO agreements, multilateral environmental agreements, and decisions of international bodies. Students who have not read Article 253's full text will restrict its scope to bilateral treaties and mark Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 253 is India's treaty implementation provision and one of the most significant centralising provisions in federal legislative relations.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 253 gives Parliament the power to legislate on ANY subject (including State List subjects) to implement international obligations. State exclusivity in the State List yields to international treaty obligations.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 253's scope is broader than bilateral treaties. It explicitly covers 'treaties, agreements, and conventions with any other country or countries' AND 'decisions made at any international conference, association or other body.' UN conventions, WTO agreements, TRIPS, and climate change accords all fall within Article 253's scope.
• Statement 3 — Correct: No state consent is needed — this is the defining difference from Article 252 (state-initiated) and makes Article 253 the most unilateral of the Centre's special legislative powers over State List subjects.

Value Addition:
• The 'real and substantial' connection test (BALCO angle) ensures Article 253 cannot be invoked for legislation only tangentially connected to an international obligation.
• India's commitments under TRIPS were implemented using Article 253 — affecting patent law (State List adjacent areas).
• Paris Agreement on climate change and CBD (Convention on Biological Diversity) obligations can be legislated under Article 253.

solution.concept_anchor: Residuary power — State List has none
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Canada's residuary power is with the federal Parliament (like India) may think Canada is the odd one out in a group of countries where residuary power is with sub-national units.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute: countries where residuary legislative power rests with the sub-national units (states/provinces).
USA: 10th Amendment — residuary power with states. Fits the group.
Australia: Section 107, Constitution of Australia — residuary power with states. Fits the group.
Switzerland: Federal system — residuary power with cantons (sub-national units). Fits the group.
Canada: Residuary power with the federal Parliament, NOT with provinces. Canada is the odd one out in a group of federal systems where residuary power is sub-nationally located.
Option (b) Canada is the odd one out — correct answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who have studied India's residuary power comparison with Canada (residuary centrally located) may mistake India for the odd one out in this group, not recognising that the question places four countries including Canada (which like India has central residuary power). However, since India is not in the option set, the test is purely about which of the four listed countries differs — Canada is the only one with central residuary power among the four.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests comparative federal knowledge about the location of residuary legislative power across federal systems.

• Option (a) USA: The 10th Amendment to the US Constitution reserves powers not delegated to the federal government to the states or the people — residuary with sub-national units.
• Option (b) Canada: The Constitution Act 1867 vests residuary legislative power in the federal Parliament — residuary with the centre. Canada is the ODD ONE OUT.
• Option (c) Australia: Under the Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act, residuary powers rest with the states — sub-national location.
• Option (d) Switzerland: The Swiss federal system reserves residuary cantonal (sub-national) competence — residuary with cantons.

In USA, Australia, and Switzerland, residuary power is with sub-national units. Canada (and India) vest it centrally. Canada is the odd one out.

Value Addition:
• India's residuary power model is most closely aligned with Canada's — both vest it centrally.
• This comparison is directly tested as a UPSC trap — students often claim India is unique in having central residuary power, forgetting Canada shares this feature.
• Germany also has a form of federal legislative hierarchy where federal law generally prevails, though the residuary structure differs.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 371A — Nagaland customary law legislative veto
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Parliament has broad power over states (including under Article 249) may assume the Rajya Sabha resolution route is available universally without knowing Article 371A carves out an explicit exception for Nagaland.
elimination_logic: The scenario concerns Parliament passing a law on Naga customary law and land ownership without the Nagaland Assembly's resolution — this directly implicates Article 371A.

Eliminate option (a): While Article 249 allows Parliament to legislate on State List subjects, Article 371A creates a specific constitutional override — Parliament cannot apply such law to Nagaland's customary law without the State Assembly's resolution, even with a Rajya Sabha resolution.
Eliminate option (b): Pith and substance is used to determine if a law validly falls within legislative competence — it does not override the specific protection in Article 371A.
Eliminate option (d): Article 252 (state-initiated legislation) is not the relevant provision — the scenario concerns Parliament legislating WITHOUT state consent.

Option (c) is correct: Article 371A explicitly provides that no Parliamentary law relating to Nagaland's customary law and practices, ownership of land, and related matters shall apply unless the State Legislative Assembly so decides — this directly invalidates the Parliamentary law in the scenario.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) is the trap — it invokes Article 249, which is a well-known provision for Parliamentary legislation on State subjects. Students who know Article 249's procedure may assume it can override everything, not knowing that Article 371A is a specific constitutional carve-out that even a valid Rajya Sabha resolution cannot override. The entity-swap here is between Nagaland's special constitutional protection and general Article 249 power.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 371A creates asymmetric federalism for Nagaland, giving its State Assembly a legislative veto over Parliamentary laws on specific subjects.

Applicable principle: Article 371A — no Parliamentary law on Nagaland's customary law and practices, ownership and transfer of land and its resources, and administration of civil and criminal justice involving Naga customary law shall apply unless the Nagaland Legislative Assembly so resolves.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Article 249 enables Parliament to legislate on State List subjects via Rajya Sabha resolution, but it cannot override the specific constitutional protection of Article 371A. Special provisions override general provisions.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Pith and substance tests whether Parliament had competence to legislate — it does not resolve situations where an explicit constitutional provision limits Parliamentary competence for a specific state.
• Option (c) — Correct: Article 371A is a direct constitutional bar — the Nagaland Assembly's resolution is a constitutional prerequisite for Parliamentary law on customary law to apply to Nagaland. The Parliamentary law is constitutionally inapplicable.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Article 252 concerns Parliament legislating at the request of state legislatures — the scenario is about Parliament legislating despite the state's protected position, not with its request.

Value Addition:
• Article 371G provides identical protection for Mizo customary law in Mizoram.
• These provisions emerged from the unique tribal negotiations during Nagaland (1963) and Mizoram (1986) statehood.
• Article 371A protections are outside the Seventh Schedule lists — they function as constitutional overrides of normal legislative relations.

(d) Article 252 — because Parliament can only legislate on matters affecting Naga customary practices if the Nagaland Legislature requests such legislation

solution.concept_anchor: Sarkaria vs Punchhi — year, mandate, and key recommendations
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know the Sarkaria Commission came before the Punchhi Commission may confuse their specific recommendations and years, swapping entries B and C.
elimination_logic: Match A (Inter-State Council, Article 263): Both Sarkaria and Punchhi recommended strengthening it — but it was the Sarkaria Commission that specifically recommended its constitution (it was set up in 1990). Match to description 4.
Match B (Sarkaria Commission): Established in 1983, submitted report in 1988, recommended restoring some subjects to State List and using Article 249 sparingly — matches description 1.
Match C (Punchhi Commission): Established in 2007, submitted report in 2010, introduced 'localisation principle' for Concurrent List — matches description 3.
Match D (Non-compliance with Articles 256-257): Ground for President's Rule under Article 356 — matches description 2. Correct: A-4, B-1, C-3, D-2 → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The swap between Sarkaria and Punchhi Commission details (B and C) is the primary trap. Both deal with Centre-State relations, and students who have studied them cursorily may swap their years (1983 vs 2007), report submission years (1988 vs 2010), or specific recommendations. Option (a) swaps B and C, which will attract students with partial knowledge of these commissions.
solution.final_explanation:
Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions are the two major constitutional bodies examining Centre-State relations, frequently tested in Prelims through their specific recommendations.

• A-4 (Inter-State Council): The Sarkaria Commission's recommendation led to the constitution of the Inter-State Council in 1990. Both commissions recommended strengthening it as the primary Centre-State coordination forum.
• B-1 (Sarkaria Commission): Established in 1983, submitted its report in 1988. Key recommendations: restore some Concurrent List subjects to State List; use Article 249 sparingly; prior consultation with states before Concurrent List legislation.
• C-3 (Punchhi Commission): Established in 2007, submitted report in 2010. Introduced 'localisation principle' — Concurrent List subjects primarily local in nature should return to State List. Also recommended codifying Centre's obligation to consult states.
• D-2 (Non-compliance with Articles 256-257): Failure to comply with Union directions under Articles 256-257 is an explicit constitutional ground for invoking President's Rule under Article 356.

Value Addition:
• Neither commission's recommendations are legally binding.
• The Inter-State Council was constituted in 1990 — over 40 years after the Constitution came into force.
• Punchhi Commission's 273 recommendations are significantly more numerous than Sarkaria's.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 254(2) — Presidential assent and subsequent Parliamentary override sequence
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who correctly identify that Presidential assent comes after state enactment may assume Parliament's subsequent law comes last, not considering that the Presidential assent must precede Parliamentary override in a logical sequence.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Parliament first enacts a Central law on a Concurrent List subject — this is the baseline legislation.
Step 2: A state legislature then enacts a law on the same Concurrent List subject that conflicts with the Central law.
Step 3: The State Governor reserves the Bill for Presidential consideration under Article 200 (mandatory for Concurrent List conflict).
Step 4: The President grants assent under Article 254(2) — this saves the State law from repugnancy and allows it to prevail over the prior Central law.
Step 5: Parliament subsequently enacts a new law that overrides even the Presidential-assent-protected State law.

Correct order: 1 → 3 → 2 → 4. But re-examining: Central law (event 1) → State law enacted (event 3) → State law assented to by President (event 2) → Parliament overrides (event 4). Answer: option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is the placement of the Governor's reservation step. Students may place the Presidential assent first (before the State law is even enacted) or place Parliament's subsequent law before Presidential assent, confusing the logical necessity that Presidential assent must come after the State law is enacted but before Parliament can logically be said to 'override' an assented State law.
solution.final_explanation:
The Article 254 repugnancy sequence has a precise constitutional logic that this question tests.

Correct order: 1 → 3 → 2 → 4:
• Event 1 (Parliament enacts Central law): Parliament first legislates on the Concurrent List subject — establishing the Central law that creates the potential repugnancy.
• Event 3 (State Legislature enacts conflicting law): The State Legislature subsequently enacts a law on the same subject — prima facie repugnant under Article 254(1).
• Event 2 (President grants assent under Article 254(2)): The Governor reserves the Bill; the President grants assent — this saves the State law from repugnancy and allows it to prevail over the earlier Central law.
• Event 4 (Parliament subsequently overrides): Parliament enacts a new law that overrides even the Presidential-assent-protected State law — Parliament's legislative supremacy is never finally extinguished.

Value Addition:
• Article 254(2) assent gives State law temporary supremacy — not permanent protection.
• The saved State law remains 'state law' — it does not acquire Central law status.
• The mandatory reservation under Article 200 for Concurrent List conflicts ensures Presidential (not merely Governor's) scrutiny.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 246A GST — outside three-list scheme; Parliament exclusive on IGST
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know both A and R are factually true may incorrectly evaluate the causal relationship, believing Parliament's exclusive power over IGST is caused by something other than the constitutional design of Article 246A(2).
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? Yes — Article 246A(1) gives both Parliament and state legislatures concurrent power over GST; Article 246A(2) reserves IGST exclusively for Parliament. This creates an asymmetry where inter-state supply is only Parliament's domain.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? Yes — The constitutional design is that taxing inter-state transactions (which cross state borders) requires a unified national framework; this is why Article 246A(2) reserves IGST to Parliament alone, to prevent conflicting state-level taxation of the same inter-state transaction.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? Yes — Parliament's exclusive power over IGST (A) is explained precisely by the constitutional policy that inter-state supply cannot be subjected to fragmented state-level tax regimes, requiring a single Parliamentary authority (R).
Both A and R correct, R explains A — correct option is (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Article 246A creates a novel concurrent taxing framework for GST, but with an important carve-out giving Parliament exclusive authority over inter-state supply.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: Article 246A(1) grants both Parliament and state legislatures the power to make GST laws (CGST and SGST respectively). Article 246A(2) carves out inter-state supply (IGST) as exclusively Parliamentary — no state can levy tax on inter-state supply of goods or services.
• Reason (R) — Correct: The constitutional rationale is that taxing inter-state transactions requires a single, nationally unified framework. If states could independently tax inter-state supply, it would fragment the common market and create cascading tax effects — precisely what GST was designed to eliminate.
• Causal relationship: R correctly and causally explains A. Parliament's exclusive IGST power (A) exists because inter-state transactions need unified national taxation to prevent market fragmentation (R).

Value Addition:
• IGST is collected by the Centre and subsequently apportioned between Centre and destination state.
• The GST Council (Article 279A) recommends rates for both CGST, SGST, and IGST — making it central to cooperative federalism in taxation.
• Article 246A is the only concurrent taxing power in the Constitution — all other taxes are exclusively Union or State.

Reason (R): Taxing inter-state supply requires a single unified national framework to prevent fragmentation of the common market, which is why the Constitution reserves this power exclusively for Parliament under Article 246A(2).

solution.concept_anchor: 42nd Amendment transfers — Education, Forests, Wild Animals to Concurrent List

statement_analysis.statement: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment (1976) transferred 'Education' from the Union List to the Concurrent List, enabling states to enact education laws subject to Central laws on the same subject.
statement_analysis.reason: Education was transferred from the STATE List (not the Union List) to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment. Before 1976, Education was a State subject — the transfer reduced state exclusivity, not Union exclusivity.

statement_analysis.statement: 'Forests' was originally in the Union List and was transferred to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment, restricting Parliament's exclusive power over forest-related legislation.
statement_analysis.reason: Forests was originally in the STATE List, not the Union List. The 42nd Amendment transferred it to the Concurrent List, giving Parliament concurrent power it previously did not have over forests — not restricting Parliament.

statement_analysis.statement: The 42nd Amendment's transfer of subjects to the Concurrent List was a significant centralising measure as it allowed Parliament to legislate on subjects previously reserved for state legislatures alone.
statement_analysis.reason: This is an accurate description — transferring subjects from State List to Concurrent List allows Parliament to legislate on them, which was not previously possible. This is a centralising effect because Parliament gains power over previously exclusive state domains.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Education was in the State List before may still accept Statement 1 as broadly correct (it reached the Concurrent List) without registering that the source was Union List, not State List.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Says Education moved from Union List to Concurrent List — WRONG. Education moved from State List to Concurrent List. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Statement 2: Says Forests was in Union List before 42nd Amendment — WRONG. Forests was in State List. Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Statement 3: Correctly characterises the transfer as centralising (Parliament gains power previously belonging only to states). Statement 3 IS correct — not incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 are NOT correct — answer is (b): 1 and 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Both Statements 1 and 2 use the same trap structure: correctly identifying the destination (Concurrent List) but falsely stating the source as Union List instead of State List. A student who knows these subjects are now in the Concurrent List may not pay attention to the 'from' direction in the transfer, accepting the statements as broadly accurate. The scope-extension error is subtle — 'Union List' replaces 'State List' in an otherwise correct description.
solution.final_explanation:
The 42nd Amendment's redistribution of legislative entries is a high-frequency source of UPSC traps precisely because students know the end-state (Concurrent List) but confuse the source.

• Statement 1 — NOT Correct: Education was in the STATE List before the 42nd Amendment. It was transferred to the Concurrent List (Entry 25), not from the Union List. The Union List never contained Education.
• Statement 2 — NOT Correct: Forests was also in the STATE List (Entry 20 of the old State List) before the 42nd Amendment. It was moved to the Concurrent List as Entry 17A — Parliament gained power; nothing was taken from the Union List.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The transfer of Education, Forests, Wild Animals, and Weights & Measures from the State List to the Concurrent List was centralising — Parliament acquired concurrent legislative power over subjects previously reserved exclusively for states.

Value Addition:
• Subjects transferred by 42nd Amendment: Education (Entry 25), Forests (Entry 17A), Wild Animals & Birds (Entry 17B), Weights & Measures, Administration of Justice.
• Sarkaria Commission recommended reversing some of these transfers — not implemented.
• NEP 2020's constitutional validity partly rests on Education being in the Concurrent List since 1976.

solution.concept_anchor: Intentional lacuna vs occupied field — state can fill gaps Parliament left

statement_analysis.statement: Under the occupied field doctrine, a State law on a Concurrent List subject is void if Parliament has comprehensively legislated on that subject with the intent to cover it exhaustively, even if no specific provision of the State law contradicts a provision of the Central law.
statement_analysis.reason: This accurately states the occupied field doctrine — comprehensive Parliamentary intent to be exhaustive voids state legislation even without direct conflict, as established in Zaverbhai Amaidas v. State of Bombay.

statement_analysis.statement: Where Parliament has deliberately left gaps in its Concurrent List legislation, state legislatures are also prohibited from filling those gaps, since the field is considered 'occupied' even in respect of matters not addressed by Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: Deliberate legislative lacunae (intentional gaps) left by Parliament are NOT 'occupied field' — they are spaces Parliament intentionally left for state legislatures to fill. The occupied field doctrine voids state laws where Parliament intended comprehensive coverage, not where Parliament deliberately left room for states.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know the occupied field doctrine is broad may assume even deliberate Parliamentary gaps are 'occupied,' treating both statements as correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Core occupied field doctrine — comprehensive Parliamentary intent voids state law even without direct conflict. Correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: Deliberate Parliamentary gaps ('intentional lacunae') are NOT occupied field — Parliament signalled room for states, which is the opposite of occupying the field. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the trap — it extends the occupied field doctrine beyond its actual scope to include deliberate Parliamentary gaps. This is a scope-extension error: the occupied field doctrine covers comprehensive intent, not intentional abstention. Students who find the occupied field doctrine's counter-intuitive nature (voiding without direct conflict) may assume it goes even further and covers deliberate gaps.
solution.final_explanation:
The distinction between 'occupied field' and 'intentional lacuna' is one of the subtlest points in Centre-State concurrent legislation.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The occupied field doctrine voids a State Concurrent List law even without direct contradiction when Parliament has legislated with the intent to be comprehensive and exhaustive. The key is Parliamentary intent to occupy the field completely — established in Zaverbhai Amaidas v. State of Bombay.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: When Parliament deliberately leaves gaps in its legislation (intentional lacunae), it has NOT occupied those gaps. States may legislate in spaces Parliament intentionally left open. The critical distinction is between Parliament intending to cover everything (occupied field) versus Parliament intending to leave room for state legislation (intentional lacuna).

Value Addition:
• Courts determine 'intentional lacuna vs. occupied field' by examining the scheme, object, and purpose of the Central legislation.
• If Parliament's silence is interpreted as permission for states, it is an intentional gap; if interpreted as comprehensive coverage, it is occupied field.
• Harmonious construction principle guides courts to prefer interpretations that allow both Central and State laws to coexist where possible.

solution.concept_anchor: State legislative competence during special Parliamentary expansions — Articles 249, 250, 252, 253

statement_analysis.statement: While Parliament exercises legislative power under Article 249 (national interest resolution), State Legislatures retain concurrent power to legislate on the same State List subject.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 249 does not suspend state legislative power — it merely adds Parliamentary competence. States can legislate simultaneously on the subject during the resolution period.

statement_analysis.statement: While Parliament exercises legislative power under Article 250 (national emergency), State laws on the same subject are automatically repealed and cease to have any effect.
statement_analysis.reason: State laws are NOT repealed under Article 250 — they are merely overridden during the emergency. They revive and become operative again after the emergency ceases. 'Automatically repealed' is a misstatement of the constitutional position.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 252, after Parliament has enacted a law at the request of consenting states, non-consenting states may subsequently adopt the law by their own legislative resolution, upon which it becomes applicable to them.
statement_analysis.reason: This accurately describes the Article 252 adoption mechanism — non-consenting states can voluntarily adopt the Parliamentary law by passing a similar resolution.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 253, Parliament's power to legislate to implement international treaties is limited to subjects that are in the Concurrent List, since those are the only subjects on which both Union and states can legislate.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 253 has no such limitation — Parliament can legislate on ANY subject, including State List subjects, to implement international treaties. There is no restriction to the Concurrent List.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 as correct and Statement 4 as incorrect may also incorrectly accept Statement 2 (believing state laws lapse during emergency), leading them to count three correct statements.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Article 249 — state power continues. Correct.
Statement 2: Article 250 — state laws are suspended/overridden, NOT repealed. They revive after emergency. 'Automatically repealed' is wrong. Incorrect.
Statement 3: Article 252 — adoption mechanism for non-consenting states is accurate. Correct.
Statement 4: Article 253 — not limited to Concurrent List; covers ALL subjects including State List. Incorrect.
Two statements correct (1 and 3) — answer is (b) Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses 'automatically repealed' — a deliberate overstatement. Students who know state laws are 'overridden' during national emergency may not precisely distinguish between 'overridden' (temporary, revives later) and 'repealed' (permanent). This partial-truth trap is designed to catch students who have general knowledge of Article 250 but lack the precision to identify the specific error.
solution.final_explanation:
This question requires precise knowledge of the effects of all four special provisions on state legislative competence.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 249 adds Parliamentary competence without removing state competence. States retain concurrent power during the resolution period. Parliament merely acquires an additional legislative domain.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Under Article 250, state laws on the same subject are not repealed — they are suspended/overridden during the National Emergency. They revive once the emergency ceases. Repeal is permanent; override is temporary.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Article 252 adoption mechanism allows non-consenting states to voluntarily bring themselves within the Parliamentary law by passing a similar resolution. Once they adopt, they too become bound and lose amendment/repeal power.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Article 253 has no restriction to the Concurrent List. Parliament can legislate on any subject — including exclusive State List subjects — to implement international treaties. This is one of its most powerful and centralising features.

Value Addition:
• The distinction between 'override' and 'repeal' under Article 250 is a high-precision UPSC test point.
• Article 253 + State List = Parliament can legislate on state subjects for international obligations without any state consent.
• Under Article 249, if Parliament and state enact conflicting laws, Article 254 repugnancy rules apply to resolve the conflict.
